concepts.hook: A bone needle that mends the sky's torn meshes, the one Ennu's widow worked by the hearth every winter until her eyes failed.
The flat stone at the centre of a house's fire, the one thing no one moves, so the Spindle is said to turn around it.
A wooden bowl of tallow and sinew in which cracked kite-ribs were soaked, kept by the house that lost its youngest to the sea.
A bone thimble worn smooth on the thumb of *Ithúna* — "the Quiet Hand" — who sewed the first sail and never once pricked her finger.
A shallow pan where a household dried its salt, its white crust rising each year, and the elders read the house's age in the layers.
A knotted cord hung from the rafter with one knot for each departed member, which Hesk checks against her own count.
A clay lamp with a split rim that is kept burning for the sea-dead, because its flame has never once gone out in the wind.
A boat-shaped shuttle that passes back and forth through the warp, weaving the sailcloth that carries the Upper Sea's wind.
A pair of bone-handled shears that trimmed the goats' winter coats, now opened wide over the pole as if waiting to cut a string.
A sail so often mended that no original cloth remains, and the Spindle keeps it as proof that what is patched can still hold wind.
The plain square kite with no tail that a child flies before learning to read the wind, and so it is the first kite of every household.
A kite with two long tails that a widow flies alone on the first calm day after mourning, tails pulling in different directions.
A kite shaped like a cradle frame, flown at a birth so that the newborn can see the sky before it sees anything else.
A stacked box-kite of waxed cloth that the midwife of an island flies from the hearth to signal that a baby has come safely into the house.

concepts.gloss: The Hood of the Old Fisher
concepts.hook: A seal-skin hood with a split seam that its wearer refused to replace for forty years, now hung over the pole to keep the cold off Hesk.
A wooden foot-form around which the boots of the drowned were shaped so that they could walk the Upper Sea without slipping.
A woollen mitten that has lost its pair, which the Spindle keeps hung on a nail because someone is always looking for the other one.
A tubular bone sheath that holds the knitting needles of a household, its open mouth turned toward the north where the Reel winds.
A heavy shawl of undyed wool pulled over the shoulders of the house's oldest woman, who gives it to a new mother when the wind turns.

concepts.gloss: The Water Jar with a Lid
concepts.hook: A covered clay jar that holds the house's fresh water through the dry months, its lid tied down with rope so the Gulls cannot get in.
A dried gourd with a rope handle used to scoop water from a boat's bilge, kept on the shelf so that no house ever sinks.
Three stones set in a triangle to hold a cooking pot over the fire, which the Spindle sets above the pole to hold the sky steady.
A hand mill of two stones turning without end, so that Hesk's patience is said to be the grinding of grain that is never finished.
A tally stick notched at the height of each child in the house each year, its marks climbing toward the rafter like a boat's cut waterline.
A hide flap that closes the roof's smoke vent in a gale, the only door in the house that opens onto the sky itself.
Four goat knucklebones tossed on the hearth to settle a household dispute, the dice by which the Spindle's elders count what can and cannot be undone.
A grey sharpening stone worn into a deep hollow by three generations of knives, and the Spindle keeps it as a count of how long the house has been sharpening its tools.
A lead weight on a cord that the Kite-Wright used to find true vertical in a new house, and that still hangs straight above the pole.
A hemp coil laid flat on a dry rock, each turn of rope a year of the house, which the Gulls are said to count when they settle on it.
A coiled-reed basket with a tight lid that holds the household's bone seeds and heirloom knots, opened only when a child is named.
A linen apron stiffened with fish glue and worn only by the house's eldest cook, which creaks in the wind like a sail being tacked.
